The text observes: *"Utilizing that jhana as his foundation of calm concentration, he then redirected mindfulness of the body on to the track of insight meditation (vipassana)."* Consciousness (*viññāṇa*) is not an independent 'soul' or enduring self; it arises in dependence on contact (*phassa*) and sense objects. The practice is to distinguish between the passing objects of awareness (thoughts, feelings, sensations) and the pure, unattached quality of 'the one who knows' (*poo roo*), resting in unconditioned peace.

In 'Maha Kaccana: Master of Doctrinal Exposition', how are we advised to handle suffering (dukkha) and emotional stress?

The text teaches: *"But the Buddha has seen the origin (adi) [22] of these attainments, i.e., craving as the origin of suffering; he has seen the danger (adinava), i.e., that they are impermanent, unsatisfactory, and subject to change; he has seen the escape (nissarana) from them, i.e., Nibbana; and he has obtained the knowledge and vision by which he can distinguish the true path from the false, i.e., the Noble Eightfold Path from the wrong eightfold path."* Rather than running away from discomfort or trying to suppress it, the Thai Forest approach is to turn around and investigate suffering directly (*dukkha-sacca*). Notice that suffering is not a permanent fixture of the heart; it is a conditioned experience arising from attachment and craving (*taṇhā*). When observed with still, patient awareness, the knot of tension naturally unwinds.
